title: Written in the Genes, Not a Curse

pages.text: Sena missed four days of school during the cold July rains. He was in hospital with severe joint pain. Sena had never hidden that he lives with sickle cell disease, but near the canteen the rumours began. Fiifi lowered his voice. “Someone in my lane says that kind of bone pain comes from a family curse. And that you can catch it by sharing a desk.” Ama frowned. “Fiifi, Sena won the district Maths quiz last month. Rumours like that hurt people. Dr Quansah is here for School Health Week. Let us ask her for the facts.”

Sena had never hidden that he lives with sickle cell disease, but near the canteen the rumours began.
Fiifi lowered his voice.
“Someone in my lane says that kind of bone pain comes from a family curse.
And that you can catch it by sharing a desk.” Ama frowned.
“Fiifi, Sena won the district Maths quiz last month.
Rumours like that hurt people.
Dr Quansah is here for School Health Week.
Let us ask her for the facts.”
pages.alt: In a JHS corridor during rainy weather, Ama speaks firmly and kindly to Fiifi to stop rumours, pointing toward a School Health Week banner outside the assembly hall.

pages.text: In the science laboratory, Dr Quansah drew two red blood cells on the board. “Sickle cell disease is not an infection,” she said. “No germ causes it, so you cannot catch it by sitting together, hugging, or sharing a plate. It is inherited. It affects haemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. With normal haemoglobin, HbA, red blood cells are round and flexible, and they slip easily through the tiniest blood vessels. With sickle haemoglobin, HbS, the cells can turn stiff and curved like a sickle. This happens more when the body is cold, short of water, or short of oxygen. The stiff cells block small blood vessels, and that causes severe pain.”

“Sickle cell disease is not an infection,” she said.
“No germ causes it, so you cannot catch it by sitting together, hugging, or sharing a plate.
It is inherited.
It affects haemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen.
With normal haemoglobin, HbA, red blood cells are round and flexible, and they slip easily through the tiniest blood vessels.
With sickle haemoglobin, HbS, the cells can turn stiff and curved like a sickle.
This happens more when the body is cold, short of water, or short of oxygen.
The stiff cells block small blood vessels, and that causes severe pain.”
pages.alt: Dr Quansah illustrates round flexible red blood cells gliding through a vessel versus stiff crescent-shaped cells jamming at a narrow vessel junction.

pages.text: Fiifi raised his hand. “Doctor, if both parents look healthy, how can their child have it?” Dr Quansah drew a square with four boxes. “This is heredity. Every child receives one haemoglobin gene from the mother and one from the father. The pair you receive is your genotype. A person with the genotype HbAS is a carrier. Carriers have sickle cell trait, and most live healthy lives. Now suppose both parents are HbAS. In each pregnancy there is a 25% chance of HbAA, a 50% chance of HbAS, and a 25% chance of HbSS. HbSS is sickle cell disease. The chances start afresh with every pregnancy, like tossing a coin again.”

pages.alt: Close-up clear educational illustration of a genetic Punnett square crossing Mother (HbAS) and Father (HbAS), showing resulting boxes HbAA (25%), HbAS (50%), and HbSS (25%).

pages.text: In Social Studies, the teacher linked the science to family life. “Sadly, when a child is born with HbSS, some families blame the mother or accuse an elder of witchcraft,” he said. “That stigma is unfair, and it is false. Heredity shows that the father and the mother each passed on one HbS gene. That is why young adults are encouraged to know their genotype. A simple blood test and genetic counselling help a couple understand their results before they plan a family. The aim is never to blame or reject anyone. It is to help people make informed choices and get good care.”

pages.text: In RME, Rahma led a reflection on dignity and compassion. “Blaming a sick child or a mother for inherited genes is false, and it is wrong,” she said. “Christians believe every person is wonderfully made in God’s image, and they are told to carry one another’s burdens. Muslims are taught never to mock the sick, and that caring for them earns reward from Allah. And in our Ghanaian tradition, a person stands strong when the community stands beside them. Stigma has no place in this class.” Fiifi looked at his desk. Then he asked quietly, “Can I copy the notes for Sena?”

pages.alt: Rahma addressing her JHS 3 classmates warmly while students prepare a welcoming revision-notes folder and a hydration reminder chart for their classroom.

pages.text: When Sena came back on Monday, Fiifi was the first to greet him. He handed over neat notes from every lesson Sena had missed. With their class teacher, the students agreed a few simple rules that were good for everyone. Water bottles were allowed on desks. Cardigans were allowed on cold, rainy mornings. And anyone who felt unwell could rest without being forced out into the heat. Sena walked to the board and solved the hardest simultaneous equation in two minutes flat. A genetic condition may shape the care a person needs. It never decides how bright they are, or how far they will go.

activities.question: Why can you not "catch" sickle cell disease by sitting beside a classmate or sharing food?
options: It is inherited from parents through genes, not caused by germ infections
Only mosquitoes transmit sickle haemoglobin during the dry season
Boiling drinking water removes haemoglobin genes before lunch

activities.question: If both parents are healthy carriers with genotype HbAS, what is the probability in each pregnancy that their child will inherit HbSS?
options: 0% because healthy parents cannot pass on HbS

activities.question: Why is blaming only the mother when a child has Sickle Cell Disease HbSS scientifically false?
options: Haemoglobin genes are inherited exclusively from grandfathers
A child with HbSS received one HbS gene from the father and one from the mother
Diet during primary school changes a child’s genotype from HbAA to HbSS

activities.question: Apply it: On a cold morning during PE, a classmate who has sickle cell disease says pain is starting in his legs. What is the best thing to do?
options: Move away from him so that you do not catch it
Tell him to run harder so that the pain goes away
Tell the teacher at once and help him rest, keep warm, and drink water

activities.prompt: Put the steps that explain a sickle cell pain episode and its care in the correct order.
items: A child inherits one HbS gene from each parent, resulting in genotype HbSS.
Dehydration, cold, or low oxygen triggers red cells to sickle and stiffen.
Stiff sickled cells clog small capillaries, causing tissue pain and crisis.
Prompt hydration, pain relief, and clinic care help the crisis subside.

activities.definition: The biological passing on of genetic traits and characteristics from parents to their offspring through genes.
distractors: The spreading of bacterial or viral infections through coughing and sneezing
The digestion of iron-rich leafy vegetables inside the small intestine

glossary.definition: The iron-containing protein inside red blood cells that binds oxygen in the lungs and transports it to body tissues.
The transmission of genetic traits (such as blood group or haemoglobin genotype) from parents to offspring.
The specific genetic makeup of an individual for a particular trait, such as HbAA, HbAS, HbAC, HbSC, or HbSS.
An individual (such as someone with HbAS) who possesses one recessive allele for a condition without having the disease, yet can pass that allele to offspring.
Unfair social disapproval, shame, or discrimination directed at someone because of a health condition or difference.
